meta.title: The Man They Sent Away
meta.skill_frame: Literary text: weigh a discredited speaker's account against the town's, and see what each one leaves out.

reader.who: Older students who read at about a fourth-grade level.
reader.why_this_level: Measured FK 6.0, 5.4 and 6.7 over the three parts (111, 135 and 110 words). The load is three speakers, a funeral, and one clue about the lawyer's standing that the reader has to track into the last part.
reader.tone: Adult subject. Plain sentences. The lesson must not make the reader feel small.

source.basis: Adapted from Willa Cather's story 'The Sculptor's Funeral' in The Troll Garden (1905), public domain in the United States.
source.attribution: Cather, Willa. The Troll Garden, and Selected Stories (1905). Project Gutenberg ebook 346. https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/346 (accessed 2026-11-12).
source.adaptation: Split long sentences, cut the dialect spellings, compressed the long funeral speech to its three claims, and dropped the minor characters. No fact or event was added.
source.survey: Cather's town funeral where the men who run the town speak over the man who left it. Chosen over a mining-camp story because the speakers' standing is visible in the scene itself.
source.avoided: No invented town name, no price, no details of the sculptor's work beyond what the story gives.

session.difficulty_basis: three speakers at one funeral, and a lawyer the town has already written off

passage.part_1: The town sent a group of men to the station siding to meet the night train. The train was twenty minutes late. Snow lay thick on the tracks, and the bluffs beyond the meadows made soft grey curves against the sky. The men stood first on one foot and then on the other, hands deep in their pockets, and talked in low voices, glancing along the river as if none of them knew what was expected of him. One man kept apart from the group. He walked to the far end of the platform, came back to the station door, and paced the track again, his chin sunk in his collar.
passage.part_2: A spare old man in a faded army coat shuffled after him. He asked whether anyone from the East would come with the body. The big man said he did not know. The old man said it was too bad the dead man had not belonged to some lodge, since a lodge funeral seemed more fitting for a person of reputation. The big man turned on his heel and walked away without a word. The old man went back to the group and said the lawyer had been drinking again. Then the whistle sounded, and the train came in red and steaming out of the dark. The coffin was lifted down onto the snowy platform. The townsmen drew back and formed a close half-circle around it, looking at the palm leaf on the lid.
passage.part_3: A young man stepped down from the express car. He had come from Boston with the body, and he asked whether the dead man's brothers were there. The red-bearded lawyer said the family was scattered. Nobody in the crowd spoke to the young man, so he rode up the long hill with the undertaker rather than in the carriage offered to him. At the house the next day, the banker and the merchant spoke at length about their own standing in the town. Then the lawyer rose, and said the town had hated the one boy who got away, because he had not wanted what it had to sell.

items.prompt: What does the old soldier wish the dead man had belonged to?

tutor_only.confirm: Right. A lodge, so that he could have had an order funeral.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The old soldier says it was too bad the dead man had not belonged to some lodge.
tutor_only.tell: The old soldier wishes the dead man had belonged to a lodge. He wanted an order funeral.
help: The sentence about this sits in the passage. Read it again.
Name the fact the passage gives, then say what it shows.
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: the student says a church or a family
if_they_say.ask: The passage names a lodge. What kind of funeral goes with a lodge?

items.prompt: The townsmen close round the coffin and none of them speaks to the young man. What does that show about who belongs?

tutor_only.confirm: Right. The townsmen belong there, and the man who came with the body does not.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The group forms a half-circle round the coffin, and nobody in the crowd speaks to the young man from Boston.
tutor_only.tell: The townsmen close round the coffin and leave the young man outside the group. He came with the body and does not belong.
help: The sentence about this sits in the passage. Read it again.
Name the fact the passage gives, then say what it shows.
tutor_only.core_idea: the townsmen belong and the young man does not
accept_ideas: the young man is an outsider
they leave him out of the group
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: the student says the young man is rude or proud
if_they_say.ask: The passage says nothing about how he behaves. Who speaks to him?

not_required: where the young man sleeps that night

items.prompt: The lawyer says the town hated Merrick for not wanting what it had to sell. What does that explain about the other two speeches?

tutor_only.confirm: Right. The banker and the merchant praised their own standing, which is the thing he refused.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The banker and the merchant speak at length about their own standing in the town, and the lawyer says the town hated the boy who did not want what it had to sell.
tutor_only.tell: The two speeches are about the speakers' own standing. That is the thing Merrick did not want.
help: The sentence about this sits in the passage. Read it again.
Name the fact the passage gives, then say what it shows.
tutor_only.core_idea: the speeches are about the speakers' own standing, which Merrick did not want
accept_ideas: they were praising themselves, not him
their speeches show what he left
they measured him by their own place in the town
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: the student says the two men praised Merrick's work
if_they_say.ask: Check who the speeches are about. Whose standing do they describe?

partial.when: the student says the speeches were long or boring
partial.ask: Length is not the point. What were the speeches about?

items.prompt: They look 'as if none of them knew what was expected.' What does that say about the waiting?

tutor_only.confirm: Right. They do not know what is expected, so the waiting is a duty, not grief.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The men look 'as if none of them knew what was expected of him,' so the waiting is a duty nobody has explained, not grief.
tutor_only.tell: The phrase says they do not know what is expected. The waiting is a duty, not grief.
help: The phrase says what the men know, not how sad they are.
If they do not know what is expected, the waiting is a duty.
tutor_only.core_idea: A duty none of them understands.
accept_ideas: a duty none of them understands
they are waiting without knowing what they are supposed to do
it is a duty, not grief
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: the student says it shows they are cold
if_they_say.ask: Cold is stated plainly. The phrase is about what they know, not how they feel.

partial.when: the student says it shows they are sad about the death
partial.ask: The phrase says what they know, not what they feel. Which one does it describe?

partial.when: The student says the waiting looks uncertain, awkward, or confused, without saying it is a duty nobody explained.
partial.ask: The phrase is about what they know. What do they not know?

tutor_only.full_idea: They do not know what is expected, so the waiting is an unexplained duty, not grief.

items.prompt: The town's leading men speak at the funeral, and the lawyer answers them. Whose account of Merrick does the story support?

tutor_only.confirm: Right. The lawyer's, because he knew Merrick and lost the same chance.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The lawyer went to school with Merrick, names what each man wanted from him, and says the town hated the one boy who got away. The town calls him a drunk.
tutor_only.tell: The story supports the lawyer. He knew Merrick, and the town's standing is not evidence about the man.
help: The sentence about this sits in the passage. Read it again.
Name the fact the passage gives, then say what it shows.
accept_ideas: the drunk lawyer tells the truth
the lawyer, since he actually knew him
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: the student says the banker's account, because he is respected
if_they_say.ask: Respect is not knowledge. Which speaker had known Merrick since school?

partial.when: the student says both accounts are equal
partial.ask: One speaker knew the man and one did not. Which one carries evidence?

tutor_only.full_idea: the lawyer's, because he knew Merrick and the others did not
